prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout: very near hands/arms occupy the lower edge (about 0.2–0.6 m), a large person or torso fills much of the upper and central view (roughly 0.4–1.2 m), and the dark upper background is farther away (approximately 2 m or more). Across frames 1–3, the large foreground person shifts from left/overhead toward the centre and then partly out of view, while the nearer lower-edge limbs change position; frames 4–5 show a more open central area and a nearby form entering from the right. Overlap between the bright lower limbs and the mid-depth person indicates substantial occlusion, with both bodies partly cropped by the image boundaries. This relative near/far ordering is much clearer than in the very dark RGB, but the map has no metric calibration, blurred boundaries, and implausibly smooth depth patches, so the metre estimates and separations between touching or overlapping people are unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates a large person mask spanning the left, upper, and central portions of frames 1–3, generally within about 0.4–1.2 m of the camera wearer and partly outside the top and side boundaries. Frame 2 contains a second differently coloured person-shaped region in the lower centre-right, overlapping the first mask and likely less than about 0.5 m from it in image-space, although their true separation and front/behind order are not recoverable from segmentation alone. In frame 4, a green region labelled “mouse” appears near the lower centre-right at roughly arm’s-reach distance, while frame 5 contains no detected instance; comparison with the RGB makes this label look unreliable and possibly a misclassified hand or nearby object. The masks clarify occupied versus open image regions and occlusions that are hard to see in the RGB, but missed limbs, holes, merged body regions, abrupt disappearance, and the “mouse” classification make identity, distance, facing direction, and gaze unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects two magenta hand skeletons in frame 1, one left of centre and one farther right, both apparently about 0.3–0.7 m from the camera and separated laterally by roughly 0.2–0.5 m. In frame 2, a single hand appears lower and left of centre; in frame 3 only a small partial hand trace remains near the centre, and frames 4–5 have no detected pose, indicating motion, occlusion, cropping, or detection failure rather than confirmed absence. These landmarks reveal finger and hand orientation that is nearly invisible in the dark RGB and show the hands shifting leftward/downward before disappearing, but no yellow body skeleton is recovered, so torso orientation, which way people face, gaze toward the camera, and who each hand belongs to cannot be established. The broken or incomplete joints, missing bodies, and rapid loss of detections make exact reach, depth, and hand-to-person associations unreliable.
